title: The line of the blind
hookLine: brahmins who've never seen Brahma are a line of blind men, each holding the one in front

lines: TWO STUDENTS, ARGUING ON A WALK.
cards: Two young brahmins, Vasettha and Bharadvaja, are out walking near a village in Kosala, stretching their legs, and arguing. The question is a serious one in their world: which path leads to union with Brahma?
Each says it's the path his own teacher teaches. Neither can convince the other. Then they remember that the Buddha is staying nearby, in a mango grove by the river Aciravati.
Let's ask him. That conversation is the thirteenth long discourse.

teach.b: Vasettha puts it generously. All these teachers' paths, he says, maybe they're like the many roads near a village: different routes, all arriving at the same place. The Buddha doesn't argue with the picture.
Vasettha, has any of the brahmins who know the three Vedas seen Brahma face to face? No. Their teachers?
No. Their teachers' teachers, back seven generations? No.
The ancient sages who composed the verses, did they ever say: we know where Brahma is, we have seen him? No.

teach.h: EACH HOLDING THE ONE IN FRONT
teach.b: Then, the Buddha says, it's like a line of blind men, each holding on to the one in front. The first one doesn't see. The one in the middle doesn't see.
The last one doesn't see. The Pali is andhaveni: a line, a braid, of the blind. Two things are worth holding carefully here.
First, this is a conversation in its own time, between the Buddha and two students, about the specific claims of their teachers.
Hindu traditions today understand Brahma, Brahman and the Vedas in many ways, and this text isn't a verdict on them.
Second, the image cuts for everyone, Buddhists included.
Any teaching passed hand to hand, by people who trust the person in front, can become a line of the blind. The Buddha's question works as a test. Has anyone in the chain actually seen?
Can you see for yourself? And he doesn't stop at criticism. The conversation goes on, and tomorrow he describes a path the young men can walk and check for themselves.

how: Buddhist teachers in many schools encourage students to test teachings against their own experience, citing discourses like DN 13 and the Kalama Sutta, while still valuing lineage and the guidance of experienced teachers.

o: a road that leads to union with Brahma
a line of the blind, each holding the next
a braid of hair worn by brahmin students

games.q: the line of the blind: tap the pairs.

s: the Buddha begins by mocking the students' teachers
he begins by asking about evidence: has anyone in the line seen Brahma?
the conversation is set near the river Aciravati in Kosala
the Buddha was staying in a mango grove there.
the image only applies to other people's teachings
any teaching passed hand to hand without anyone seeing can become a line of the blind, Buddhist ones included.

games.q: you're the Buddha. two students ask which path leads to union with Brahma. what do you ask first?
o: has anyone in your teachers' line seen Brahma?
games.why: he traces the line back seven generations and to the ancient sages, and finds no one who claimed to have seen. then he uses the image of a line of the blind.

practice: Choose something you were taught and never checked, about money, people or yourself, and picture the line it came down: from whom, and from whom before that.
Then ask the Buddha's question: has anyone in this line actually seen it, and have I? You don't have to throw it away; just hold it as untested for now, and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Andhaveni. A teaching passed hand to hand, each trusting the one in front, with no one who has seen for themselves. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali andhaveni: a line of the blind, each holding the one in front. veni also means a braid.

carryVoice: Your line: can you see for yourself? The question works on every chain, your own included. That's day five hundred forty-one.
